The Black-faced sheathbill (Chionis minor) is a distinctive scavenger of the sub-Antarctic islands, whose life history is shaped by a harsh and unpredictable environment. Field observations indicate that females typically produce a single clutch of eggs each year [F_R_i = single clutch of eggs each year], a low reproductive frequency that reflects the energetic constraints of foraging in a cold, windy climate. Within each nesting attempt, the clutch size is most often one egg [N_R_i = the clutch size is most often one egg], though two-egg clutches are occasionally recorded during years of exceptional prey abundance. Under the thermal conditions of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C], which approximate the active metabolic temperature of the adult bird during incubation, the eggs exhibit a maximum reproductive rate that translates to a remarkably modest annual output, consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes adult survival over high fecundity. The nestling period is characterized by steady but slow growth, constrained by the sporadic availability of marine invertebrates and carrion.

Newly hatched chicks emerge at a remarkably low wet weight of 25 grams [Wwb = 25 grams], representing a small fraction of the eventual adult mass and necessitating an extended period of intensive parental provisioning. This modest birth mass is consistent with the semi-altricial developmental mode typical of the family Chionididae, where the downy chick is capable of limited mobility but remains entirely dependent on the attending adults for both food and thermoregulation. The eggs, which are laid directly on the ground in a simple scrape nest, are incubated for a period ranging between 24 and 30 days. Specifically, the age at birth is approximately 30 days [ab = approximately 30 days] under controlled incubation at a constant 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a temperature that reflects the optimal artificial incubation conditions used successfully for several other charadriiform species. The hatchlings must quickly develop the capacity to process solid food items delivered by the parents, as the endogenous yolk reserves are depleted within the first few days of exogenous life.

Following the initial weeks of rapid mass gain, the nestling begins a phase of feather development that culminates in the achievement of powered flight. For Black-faced sheathbills maintained at the standard active metabolic temperature of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C], this fledging milestone occurs at 55 days after hatching [tx = 55 days after hatching]. This relatively extended period spent in the nest is characteristic of species that must develop strong flight muscles and insulating plumage before facing the cold, windy conditions of their coastal habitat. The fledgling then undergoes a post-fledging dependency phase during which it continues to receive supplemental feedings from the parents while refining its foraging skills. The transition to nutritional independence is a gradual process, and young birds often remain in close proximity to the natal territory for several additional weeks as they learn to locate the intertidal invertebrates and carrion that constitute the bulk of the adult diet before dispersing to establish their own home ranges.

Under the thermal conditions of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C], which represent the typical body temperature of an active adult, the time since birth at puberty is estimated at 165 days [tp = 165 days]. Young birds can thus acquire the morphological and physiological characteristics of a sexually mature individual within the same calendar year in which they hatched, a developmental pace that allows them to prospect for breeding territories during the austral summer immediately following their birth. However, the onset of actual breeding behavior is typically deferred, as first-year birds must navigate competition for high-quality nesting sites and establish pair bonds. The early achievement of puberty, nevertheless, provides a crucial buffer in an environment where adult mortality from storms, predation by skuas, and food scarcity can create frequent opportunities for young birds to fill vacancies in the breeding population.

The lifespan of the Black-faced sheathbill in the wild has been documented to reach up to 20 years [am = up to 20 years] at a body temperature of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C], a substantial longevity given the species' small body size and the challenging conditions of its sub-Antarctic habitat. This extended lifespan is consistent with a "slow" life-history pace, characterized by low annual fecundity, high adult survivorship, and deferred reproductive effort. Most individuals delay their first breeding attempt until their second calendar year, a strategy that allows them to acquire the foraging experience and social status necessary to successfully raise a single chick to fledging. The ultimate wet weight for females, which represents the asymptotic body mass for nestlings as they approach adult size, reaches a maximum of 635 grams [Wwi = 635 grams]. This substantial size, combined with a long life and low reproductive output, positions the species as a classic example of an equilibrium-oriented life history finely tuned to the extreme seasonal productivity of its island environment.
